editorNote: A galaxy fits inside the BBC Micro this week, while other game makers find new worlds in history, fantasy and the classroom.
morningLine: This week in 1984: Elite takes off, and the computer-game horizon suddenly looks vast.

milestone.title: Elite launches on the BBC Micro
milestone.note: Its open-ended 3D trading-and-combat world helped define the space-simulation genre and demonstrated how expansive a home-computer game could feel.

lead.headline: Elite Opens a Galaxy of Trade and Combat on the BBC Micro
lead.dek: Acornsoft’s new space game turns a 32K home computer into an open-ended universe.
body: Acornsoft releases Elite for the BBC Micro on September 20, opening a new kind of journey at the home-computer keyboard. Ian Bell and David Braben have built a space game in which a pilot can trade, fight and roam rather than simply chase a fixed score. The ship begins with the humble rank of Harmless; the coveted destination is Elite.

The view from the cockpit is a wireframe three-dimensional world, its ships and stations drawn in spare, sharp lines. Behind those lines sits a startling expanse: eight galaxies of 256 worlds each. Procedural generation makes that scale possible on a BBC Micro with just 32K of memory, leaving the player with the impression of a much larger universe than the machine’s specifications suggest.

Trading cargo between systems offers one route upward, while combat and riskier choices promise others. Elite asks players to make their own stories from those decisions. It is not an arcade round with three lives and a final score; it is a continuing career, with every docking and departure another chance to change its course.

The launch package helps carry that fiction beyond the screen. Alongside the game come manuals, a ship-recognition chart and Robert Holdstock’s novella The Dark Wheel. A later contemporary Beebug review lists the cassette at £14.95 and the disc at £17.65, including VAT. For players opening the box this week, the smallest BBC Micro now holds a remarkably large frontier.

stories.headline: Seven Cities of Gold Sends Players Across an Uncharted Map
body: In its September review, COMPUTE! turns to The Seven Cities of Gold, Ozark Softscape and Electronic Arts’s exploration game. A player outfits a voyage in Spain, sails west and weighs trade, settlement and conflict in the Americas. Food and crew matter as much as any discovery, giving the journey the hazards of an expedition rather than a simple screen-by-screen contest.

Reviewer James V. Trunzo counts more than 2,800 screens and notes a utility for generating new continents. The Atari edition is available at $39.95, with a Commodore 64 version described as forthcoming. The review is evidence of the game’s presence on September shelves, not a claim that it launched this particular week.

stories.headline: Ultima III Turns Fantasy Quest into a Four-Character Expedition
body: The September COMPUTE! review of Exodus: Ultima III finds a fantasy campaign built around a party rather than a lone hero. Players may assemble up to four adventurers from five races and eleven professions, and keep twenty characters on a disk. Spell books, a playbook, quick-reference guide and cloth map make the box feel like a portable campaign kit.

Origin Systems lists the game at $59.95, with editions for Apple II, Atari 400/800, Commodore 64, IBM PC and PCjr. Reviewer David K. Peacock praises its graphics and music while noting that combat and repeated dungeon journeys can slow the expedition.

stories.headline: Word Flyer Makes Reading Practice a Shared Game
body: Electronic Arts ChildWare’s Word Flyer gives Atari owners a joystick-driven lesson that puts two players on the same side. Rather than competing, they build a cumulative score together, steering through letter and word exercises drawn from a built-in list of more than 2,000 words.

A September COMPUTE! review describes early levels built around letters and two-letter words, then more advanced matching. The 48K disk edition is listed at $35 for Atari 400/800 and XL machines. Its cooperative scoring is an unusual choice on a shelf full of contests.

stories.headline: The Fat Mac Gives Macintosh Four Times the Memory
body: Apple’s Macintosh 512K, introduced September 10, remains fresh in shop-window discussion this week. The compact computer keeps its nine-inch monochrome display, 400K floppy drive and 8 MHz Motorola 68000, but expands built-in RAM from 128K to 512K.

That fourfold memory increase gives graphical programs and documents more breathing room. It is context from the preceding week, not a new September 17-23 announcement; shoppers now have a roomier version of the machine Apple launched in January.

worldAnchor.headline: Bomb Strikes U.S. Embassy Annex Near Beirut
worldAnchor.summary: A September 20 van bombing at the U.S. Embassy annex northeast of Beirut killed at least 23 people, according to the following day’s Washington Post report; early casualty figures were provisional.
